title: Aisha Wahab Becomes First Afghan American in Congress After Winning California Special Election
excerpt: The progressive California state senator defeats Melissa Hernandez to succeed Eric Swalwell, overcoming nearly $4.4 million in AIPAC-aligned spending.
body:
• California State Senator Aisha Wahab has won the special election to succeed former Rep. Eric Swalwell in California's 14th Congressional District.
  • Wahab, 39, becomes the first Afghan American to serve in the U.S. Congress.
  • She defeated Bay Area Rapid Transit Board President Melissa Hernandez 53% to 47%, overcoming nearly $4.4 million in spending by AIPAC-aligned super PACs.
  • The two will face off again in November's general election for a full two-year term.

First Afghan American in Congress

California State Senator Aisha Wahab has won a special election to fill the U.S. House seat vacated by former Rep. Eric Swalwell, the Associated Press projected Thursday. Wahab becomes the first Afghan American to serve in Congress.

https://x.com/clashreport/status/2090716537027952969

Wahab defeated Melissa Hernandez, president of the Bay Area Rapid Transit Board of Directors, by a margin of 53.1% to 46.9% in the August 18 runoff. The result was called two days after election night, as preliminary counts had been too close to call immediately.

"From foster care to Congress, this journey shows the possibility of the American Dream. I will fight for this district that raised me."

— Aisha Wahab, in a statement after her projected victory

Wahab, a progressive Democrat, will represent the state's 14th Congressional District, which covers parts of Alameda County on the eastern side of the San Francisco Bay. She will serve out the remainder of Swalwell's term through January, and the two candidates will face each other again in the November general election for a full two-year term.

AIPAC's Millions Fall Short

The Bay Area race became the latest flashpoint in the Democratic Party's internal divisions over Israel. AIPAC's super PAC arm, United Democracy Project, injected nearly $2 million in advertising attacking Wahab and supporting Hernandez, with another $1.9 million from BOLD America, a group that also receives AIPAC funding. In total, AIPAC-aligned groups spent roughly $4.4 million in the race.

The ad campaigns largely avoided Middle East policy, instead targeting Wahab's record on public safety. In response, American Priorities, a super PAC formed to counter AIPAC spending, spent more than $200,000 supporting Wahab.

Wahab has called for cutting U.S. military aid to Israel and said at a candidate forum that she believes the war in Gaza constitutes a genocide. Hernandez said Israel has a right to defend itself while adding that "the destruction in Gaza has gone too far." Neither candidate made Israel a central campaign issue.

"I'm very proud of this district for not listening to the hate-mongering and really knowing and believing the work that I've done," Wahab told KQED on election night.

From Foster Care to the Capitol

Wahab, 39, made history in 2022 when she became the first Muslim and Afghan American elected to the California State Senate. Before that, she was the first Afghan American elected to public office in the United States, winning a Hayward City Council seat in 2018.

Her campaign focused on affordable housing, protecting Medicare, banning congressional stock trading, and supporting small businesses. She was backed by the Congressional Progressive Caucus.

Swalwell, a Democrat who had been running for California governor, resigned from Congress in April amid sexual assault allegations, which he denies. Criminal investigations into the allegations are ongoing. Over the past weekend, federal agents seized electronic devices from Swalwell at the San Francisco airport and later searched his home in Washington, D.C.

What's Next

Wahab's victory narrows the House vacancy count and gives Democrats 213 seats to Republicans' 218. The solidly Democratic district is expected to remain competitive in November, when Wahab and Hernandez will again appear on the ballot for the full term. AIPAC's defeat in the special election may not deter renewed spending in the general election, given the organization's pattern of investing heavily in races that signal its willingness to oppose progressive candidates.
